verdicts.summary: Env, host-token and usage-limit secret names and redaction output match the removed per-kind code. The only gap is the hand-kept driver map, which is finding 0. Today all nine built-in drivers are in the map, so finding 0 has no current effect.
A rollback to the parent build leaves the marker in settings.json as the Antigravity API key, and the real key is stranded in the store under a name the old build never reads.
verdicts.scenario: 1) Run this build with an Antigravity apiKey saved in settings.json. The load migration moves it to the store and rewrites settings.json with "apiKey": "••••••". 2) Downgrade to the parent build. 3) The old build decodes the marker as a plain string and the Antigravity driver passes it as GEMINI_API_KEY. The real key stays in the store under provider-config-... which the old build never reads.
verdicts.consequence: After a rollback, Gemini API key auth for the Antigravity instance fails with the marker as the key. The user has to re-enter the key. The parent build had no secret handling for this field.

verdicts.summary: Every server path that sends settings to clients goes through redactServerSettingsForClient, which now maps provider config secrets. The client gets the marker or "", never the stored key.
verdicts.scenario: Client calls serverGetSettings, serverUpdateSettings, subscribes to the settings stream, or reads the serverConfig snapshot. Each passes through ws.ts:1690, 2403, 2415 or 3047. Grep for other settings sends found none.

verdicts.summary: The settings-variant secret field always passes value="", so a blank edit never commits. A saved Antigravity API key can no longer be removed from the provider form.
verdicts.scenario: 1) An Antigravity instance has a saved apiKey. The form renders SecretInput with value="" and configured=true. 2) The user clicks the field, types or deletes, and blurs. The draft is "", which equals value "", so useCommitOnBlur does not call onCommit. 3) Nothing is committed, so the saved key stays.
verdicts.consequence: A saved Antigravity API key cannot be removed from the provider form. Before this change the field was a plain DraftInput with the saved value; a blank commit went through nextProviderConfigWithFieldValue with clearWhenEmpty "omit" and deleted the key. The only other way to remove it is deleting the whole instance. The source-control host form has a clear path (SourceControlHostSettings.tsx:62-66), but the provider form has none.

verdicts.summary: Both orderings keep the flag. decodeTo appends the decoding link to the target schema and keeps its context. annotateKey merges into the existing context. resolveAnnotationsKey reads that context. So secretSetting before withDecodingDefault (antigravity apiKey) and after it (managementKey, github tokens) both reach isSecretSetting.
verdicts.scenario: Build the field schema with secretSetting before withDecodingDefault and annotateKey after it, then call isSecretSetting. Also the reverse order used for managementKey and github tokens.

verdicts.summary: The removed helper had one caller, and that caller now uses secretSettingsFields. A grep of the repo, excluding .repos, finds no remaining reference to secretSourceControlHostSettingsFields or providerSettingsForm.secret. Every host field that had secret: true (github tokens, gitcafe token, bitbucket accessToken and apiToken) now carries settingsSecret, so no host secret loses protection.
verdicts.scenario: Compute SOURCE_CONTROL_HOST_SECRET_FIELDS after the removal. For github, gitcafe and bitbucket, check that secretSettingsFields still returns their secret fields.

verdicts.summary: A store read failure at startup makes getSettings fail for an Antigravity user, and the registry then starts with no provider instances at all.
verdicts.scenario: 1) An Antigravity instance has a key in the store. 2) At startup store.get fails. 3) materializeSettingsSecrets fails with ServerSettingsError (no fallback). 4) getSettings fails. 5) ProviderInstanceRegistryHydration.ts:159-165 catches it with orElseSucceed and uses an empty configMap. 6) No provider instances are registered, including the defaults, until the next settings change.
verdicts.consequence: An Antigravity user now depends on the secret store at startup. Before this change a user with no env or host secrets never read the store on load. The failure is a total loss of provider instances until the next settings save.

verdicts.summary: When the store read fails, the change stream falls back to the raw settings, so the Antigravity driver receives the marker as its API key.
verdicts.scenario: 1) The store read fails for a secret during materializeChanges. 2) Effect.catch logs and returns the raw settings, which still hold "••••••" as apiKey. 3) Subscribers (ProviderInstanceRegistryHydration.ts:121-125) reconcile with the marker as config. 4) AntigravityDriver.ts:112-115 passes it on, and antigravityAuthSupport.ts:230-232 sets GEMINI_API_KEY="••••••".
verdicts.consequence: Gemini auth for the Antigravity instance fails with the marker as the key until the next settings change. No secret is exposed. Before this change the fallback only affected host tokens and env values.

verdicts.summary: A failed store write at load leaves plaintext cached, and every later settings save then re-queues that write and fails, even for unrelated changes.
verdicts.scenario: 1) At load, the store write for an Antigravity plaintext key fails. The warning is logged and the plaintext stays in the cached settings. 2) Any later updateSettings, even one that changes an unrelated field, re-sends the cached plaintext. 3) persistSettingsSecrets sees a non-redacted value and queues a write (serverSettings.ts:960-970). 4) The store write fails again, the rollback runs, and the update returns an error.
verdicts.consequence: While the store cannot be written, every server settings save fails with a write-secret error, including unrelated changes. The plaintext key is never moved. The parent build did not write Antigravity keys to the store, so this path is new.

verdicts.summary: An older client shows the marker in its password input. If the user appends to it and commits, the marker plus the typed text is saved as the key.
verdicts.scenario: 1) An older client that does not know apiKey is secret displays the marker "••••••" in its password input. 2) The user clicks in and types a character at the end. 3) The old client commits "••••••x". 4) The server sees a non-marker value and writes "••••••x" as the key (serverSettings.ts:960-970).
verdicts.consequence: A version-skewed client can silently save a corrupted key. Low severity because it needs an old client connected to a new server.
